vignette:
She is a 77-year-old North American woman who has spent much of her life helping children make sense of their feelings as a school counselor. In her work, she has always been the calm one in the room, the person students can cry with without feeling embarrassed. That identity matters to her; it has shaped how she has moved through the world and how others have come to rely on her. Even now, widowed and living more quietly than she once did, she speaks about her career with a kind of steady pride. She has been the one to listen, to translate pain into words, to help families imagine that hard things can be survived.

The disaster that changed her came later in life, when she believed she had already weathered the most difficult seasons. It is a man-made catastrophe, sudden and senseless, and what she remembers most is not only the event itself but the instant her ordinary understanding of safety collapsed. Before that day, the world had felt predictable enough: a place where routines could be counted on, where a locked door meant protection, where people in charge were supposed to keep danger contained. When the disaster unfolds, she is caught in the confusion of it, trying to understand what is happening while people around her move with panic and disbelief. She recalls sharp sounds, voices rising, the strange unreality of not knowing whether what she is seeing is truly happening. In the moment, she does what she has always done: she tries to stay useful, to help, to keep herself composed so others can follow her lead. Later, she realizes that this instinct may have kept her functioning, but it also delayed the full weight of what she had lived through.

In the days afterward, she moves through the world as if slightly detached from it. She goes through practical tasks, answers calls, and checks on others, but inside she feels as though something has cracked open and not been repaired. Sleep becomes difficult. At first she tells herself that anyone would be unsettled after something like this, but soon she notices that her mind returns to the event again and again without her permission. Certain sounds pull her back instantly. A sudden bang, a siren, even the metallic slam of a car door can make her whole body tense before she can think. She is startled more easily now and dislikes being caught off guard. She begins to scan rooms automatically, checking exits, listening for changes in tone, watching for movement that might signal danger. She does not like how effortful this has become, how much energy it takes just to feel safe in an ordinary place.

She tries to keep her routines, because routines have always anchored her, but places that once felt familiar begin to carry a residue of threat. Crowded public buildings leave her uneasy. She avoids news reports about similar events because she cannot bear to see the images repeated, yet she also feels guilty for turning away. At times she is flooded with memories so vivid that she feels the disaster has stepped back into the room with her. Her chest tightens, her stomach drops, and she has to remind herself where she is. Other times, the memories arrive more quietly as a fog of dread. She wakes in the night with her heart racing, certain for a moment that something terrible is about to happen. When she cannot return to sleep, she lies in the dark replaying what she should have done differently, questioning whether she missed a sign, whether she could have protected someone more effectively. The self-blame is painful because it sounds, to her, like a failure of the very role she has spent a lifetime inhabiting.

Her widowed life has made the aftermath lonelier. She misses the simple reassurance of having someone nearby who knew her without explanation. She is careful not to burden her adult children, though she can see they notice how much she has changed. At family gatherings she remains pleasant and attentive, but she tires quickly and sometimes withdraws to a quieter room, needing a few minutes alone to steady herself. She still works part-time with students, and in that setting she often performs competence before she feels it. She can be warm and attentive for a child who is anxious, yet afterward she may sit in her office with the door closed, holding her breath until her body relaxes. She has become more aware of how much effort she uses to contain her reactions.

Even now, she is not entirely living in the present. Part of her remains on alert, listening for the next shock, as if danger might arrive without warning. She misses the ease she once had, the unselfconscious way she moved through hallways and parking lots and crowded rooms. At the same time, she continues to show up, to answer the phone, to make tea, to call back a student’s parent, to keep the day moving. The contrast between her outer steadiness and inner vigilance is one of the quiet burdens she carries, along with the knowledge that a single man-made catastrophe has altered the shape of safety in her life.
